patient.chief_complaint: Recurrent visual disturbances followed by severe one-sided headaches for 5 years
patient.hpi:
A 28-year-old woman presented to the neurology outpatient clinic for evaluation and management of recurrent headaches with visual symptoms that she has experienced approximately once monthly for the past 5 years. Each episode begins with a shimmering, crescent-shaped visual disturbance in the periphery of her right visual field that gradually expands into a flickering zigzag arc (fortification spectra) over 20-30 minutes, then fades. During this visual aura she cannot read effectively and describes the phenomenon as like 'looking through a kaleidoscope.' After the visual aura resolves, she develops a severe left-sided throbbing headache (8/10 intensity) with nausea, photophobia, and phonophobia lasting 6-12 hours. Vomiting occurs in approximately half of episodes. She takes ibuprofen 400 mg which only partially helps. She has not tried triptans. She denies any limb weakness, numbness, speech difficulty, or loss of consciousness associated with the episodes. Between attacks she is entirely normal.

She has a maternal aunt with similar migraines. She reports that episodes are triggered by menstruation, sleep deprivation, and skipping meals. Oral contraceptive pills were prescribed by her GP 2 years ago for dysmenorrhea but she stopped them after 6 months because she felt they increased headache frequency. She has no history of stroke, hypertension, diabetes, or cardiac disease. She is a graphic designer, non-smoker, moderate caffeine use. The frequency of attacks has increased from one every 6 weeks to almost monthly over the past year, prompting this referral.

differential.diagnosis: Migraine without aura with visual symptoms
differential.key_features: Stereotyped 20-30 min expanding fortification spectra and headache pattern are diagnostic of aura, not the variably-located cephalalgia of migraine without aura

differential.diagnosis: Focal occipital seizure with visual phenomena
differential.key_features: Visual seizures are brief (<2 min), stereotyped colored circles; 20-30 min spread is too slow for ictal propagation; no impaired awareness
5-year recurrent identical pattern, young patient, no vascular risk factors; gradual aura march is incompatible with abrupt TIA onset
No haemorrhage history, no thunderclap, no fixed deficit — would need MRI for definitive exclusion if red flags emerge

optimal_actions.action: Search guideline literature to confirm ICHD-3 1.2 criteria for migraine with aura and exclude SNOOP/CHATS red flags
optimal_actions.expected_finding: ICHD-3 criteria for migraine with aura confirmed; no SNOOP red flag present that mandates further workup

tool_parameters.query: ICHD-3 migraine with aura diagnostic criteria SNOOP red flags

optimal_actions.action: Check drug interactions and contraindications for acute (triptan/ergotamine/CGRP antagonist) and prophylactic (beta-blocker, topiramate, valproate, amitriptyline) migraine medications appropriate to this patient
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Sumatriptan 50-100 mg is appropriate as acute therapy; preventive options (topiramate, propranolol) reviewed for monthly-frequency disability

optimal_actions.action: Take a structured headache and aura history against ICHD-3 1.2: number of attacks, aura modality and full reversibility, gradual spread over at least five minutes, duration of each symptom between five and sixty minutes, unilaterality, temporal relation to the headache, and a documented red-flag review. This is the diagnostic test for this condition
optimal_actions.expected_finding: ICHD-3 1.2 criteria documented item by item against the reference set for this subtype, with the red-flag review recorded

useless_tools.rationale: Head CT is less sensitive than MRI for migraine-relevant structural causes and is not indicated in typical migraine with aura; even when imaging is warranted, MRI is preferred
Lumbar puncture is not indicated in migraine with aura; reserve for suspected SAH (with normal CT) or meningitis — neither present here
Ambulatory cardiac monitoring is not indicated in typical migraine with aura — no role unless cardioembolic stroke is on the differential
OCT is not part of the migraine workup and is reserved for demyelinating optic neuropathy or chiasmal disease — not indicated here

critical_actions: Confirm ICHD-3 1.2 criteria are met (≥2 attacks with reversible aura ≥5 min, accompanied/followed by headache within 60 min)
Document absence of SNOOP red flags (Systemic symptoms, Neurologic deficits between attacks, sudden Onset, Onset after age 50, Pattern change)
Counsel that combined oestrogen-progestogen contraception is WHO Category 4 in migraine with aura
Initiate sumatriptan 50-100 mg at headache onset (not during aura) for acute therapy
Discuss preventive therapy (topiramate or propranolol) given approximately monthly frequency
contraindicated_actions: Do not co-administer two different triptans within 24 hours
Do not co-administer triptans with ergotamines within 24 hours
Do not prescribe combined oestrogen-progestogen contraception in migraine with aura
key_reasoning_points: ICHD-3 1.2.1 is a clinical diagnosis — no neuroimaging or laboratory test confirms migraine with aura when the criteria are met

Routine brain MRI is NOT indicated in typical migraine with aura without SNOOP red flags [AAN_2000]; the MRI ordered for this case is best understood as a defensive over-investigation, not a guideline-mandated step
Two non-specific subcortical WMH on MRI are an expected (non-actionable) incidental finding in migraineurs and do not change management
Frequency at almost monthly with disability satisfies common thresholds for offering preventive therapy [Holland_2012]

red_herrings.data_point: Two non-specific subcortical white matter hyperintensities on brain MRI
red_herrings.intended_effect: May prompt unnecessary anxiety, repeat imaging, or workup for demyelinating disease
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Non-specific subcortical WMH are common in migraineurs and are not clinically actionable in the absence of inflammatory or vascular features

red_herrings.data_point: Tiny subcortical white matter T2 foci on MRI
red_herrings.intended_effect: Small white matter hyperintensities in young women can suggest MS or cerebrovascular disease
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Non-specific T2 hyperintensities are commonly seen in migraineurs; not diagnostic for MS (no periventricular distribution) or lacunar stroke (size <3 mm)

red_herrings.data_point: OCP history raising concern for cerebral venous thrombosis
red_herrings.intended_effect: OCP use + headache with visual symptoms could suggest CVT
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Patient stopped OCP 1.5 years ago; CVT would show progressive headache with papilledema or focal deficit; 5-year identical episodic history inconsistent with CVT

clinical_assessment.impression: Structured headache and aura history taken against ICHD-3 1.2. 4 of the four criterion-C characteristics are documented — the diagnosis is met on the history, which is the only test that establishes it. The distinction from a transient ischaemic attack is made here and not by imaging: aura spreads gradually over minutes and is positive before it is negative, whereas ischaemia is abrupt and negative from the outset. Imaging is for the red flags this history screens for, not for the diagnosis.

output.summary:
LITERATURE SEARCH: Triptan Use in Migraine with Aura KEY FINDINGS:
1. TRIPTANS AND AURA: Historical concern about triptans causing vasoconstriction and worsening aura; however, multiple RCTs and meta-analyses show triptans are safe and effective in migraine with aura when taken at headache onset (not during aura)
2. SUMATRIPTAN SAFETY: No increased stroke risk in women with migraine with aura taking triptans
3. CONTRAINDICATIONS: Triptans are contraindicated in hemiplegic migraine, basilar migraine, uncontrolled hypertension, ischemic heart disease, or recent (14 days) MAOI use
4. PREVENTIVE OPTIONS: Topiramate (50 mg BID), propranolol (40-120 mg BID), amitriptyline (25-75 mg QHS) are first-line preventive agents; 3 or more migraines/month with disability is threshold for preventive therapy
5. OCP AND MIGRAINE WITH AURA: Combined OCP is relatively contraindicated in migraine with aura (WHO category 3-4) due to stroke risk. Patient was correct to stop. Progestin-only pills are safe. CONCLUSION: Sumatriptan 100 mg at headache onset is appropriate; preventive therapy indicated given monthly frequency (topiramate or propranolol); avoid combined OCP. Triptans safe at headache onset (not during aura); preventive therapy indicated at ≥3/month; combined OCP relatively contraindicated in migraine with aura

DRUG INTERACTION REVIEW — SUMATRIPTAN FOR MIGRAINE WITH AURA Query: Sumatriptan safety and drug interactions FINDINGS: SUMATRIPTAN (5-HT1B/1D agonist): - Take at headache onset (not during aura phase) - Dose: 50-100 mg orally; may repeat after 2 hours if partial relief (max 200 mg/day) - CONTRAINDICATIONS: Ischemic heart disease, uncontrolled HTN, history of stroke/TIA, hemiplegic migraine, concurrent MAOI or ergotamine use - This patient: No contraindications identified POTENTIAL INTERACTIONS: - SSRIs/SNRIs + triptans: Theoretical serotonin syndrome risk; use cautiously but generally safe - Ibuprofen: No pharmacokinetic interaction; can be combined for enhanced effect NAPROXEN + SUMATRIPTAN COMBINATION: Fixed-dose combination (Treximet) shown superior to either alone CONCLUSION: Sumatriptan 100 mg safe for this patient. No current drug interactions. Naproxen sodium 550 mg co-administration may enhance efficacy. Sumatriptan 100 mg — no contraindications identified in this review; take at headache onset, not during the aura phase; sumatriptan-naproxen co-administration (fixed-dose combination or separately) has RCT evidence of superior efficacy to either agent alone in migraine
